content: In sugar chemistry, an anomer is a specific type of epimer. It is a stereoisomer, more precisely a diastereomer, of a saccharide in its cyclic form. The difference between anomers lies solely in the configuration at the hemiacetal (or hemiketal) carbon, which is also referred to as the anomeric carbon. If the hydroxyl group attached to the anomeric carbon is in the axial position, as seen in glucose, the sugar is classified as an alpha anomer. Conversely, if the hydroxyl group is in the equatorial position, the sugar is classified as a beta anomer. For instance, α-D-glucopyranose and β-D-glucopyranose, the two cyclic forms of glucose, are examples of anomers. The stabilization of the alpha anomer is influenced by the anomeric effect. The process by which the two anomers interconvert is known as mutarotation. These two anomers represent distinct chemical structures and, as a result, exhibit different physical and chemical properties, including differences in optical rotation. For example, α-D-glucose has an optical rotation of +112 degrees, while its anomer, β-D-glucose, has an optical rotation of +19 degrees.
